newsitem.title: USA: Clinton studies Kremlin shakeup on eve of summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton studies Kremlin shakeup on eve of summit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton pored over details of Russian President Boris Yeltsin's latest Kremlin power shuffle on Wednesday as he prepared for a two-day summit with Yeltsin in Helsinki starting on Thursday.

Clinton "is very, very engaged on this," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said as the president got set to depart Wednesday evening for a Finland summit expected to focus on Russia's opposition to NATO plans to extend membership to some of Moscow's onetime Warsaw Pact allies.

Yeltsin in recent days has shaken up his Cabinet in a move intended, at least in part, to re-establish his authority after long illness and to bring market-oriented economic reformers into senior Cabinet positions.

Anatoly Chubais, a prominent reformer recently restored to power as a first deputy premier, said on Tuesday the radical reshuffle was not yet over. "There will be more surprises," he told commercial NTV television.
McCurry said Clinton finds all this "fascinating" and was using much of his remaining time in Washington to study it.

"Clinton is very interested in that ... and what the implications are for our bi-lateral relationship, and how we assess the progress of reform in Russia," McCurry said. "We may be in a period of real internal dynamic change in Russia."

The president also crammed his last few hours of White House time with domestic politics, trying to break an impasse in talks with Republican congressional leaders on balancing the federal budget. Clinton also had more physical therapy for his injured right knee.
He underwent surgery last Friday to reattach a tendon torn from the knee when he caught his heel on a stair.

The Helsinki meeting marks the first personal encounter for the U.S. and Russian presidents since an April summit in Moscow. Ironically, the Finnish city replaced Washington, the venue originally scheduled, in order to make the trip less arduous for Yeltsin, who had heart by-pass surgery late last year and has struggled with double pneumonia more recently.
While he has been looking more robust of late, Clinton has essentially been confined to a wheelchair.

Released from the hospital on Sunday, he was forced to delay the start of the summit by one day and cancel plans to visit Denmark despite initial vows that the injury would not affect his summit schedule.

Senior administration officials stress that they expect no dramatic breakthroughs at the summit. Instead, they hope for progress in smoothing over divisive issues like the prospective NATO expansion and perhaps making some progress toward a charter spelling out NATO-Russia relations.
Washington also hopes to begin a new round of talks on nuclear missile reductions with Moscow, but first wants the Russian parliament to ratify the long-delayed START-2 treaty, signed in 1993.
